chunks.title: Severe bleeding
steps: Press hard directly on the wound with a clean cloth or your palm.
Keep pressing without lifting to check. Do not remove the first cloth if blood soaks through — add another on top.
Raise the injured limb above the heart if there is no suspected fracture.
Keep the person warm and lying still.
Call for medical help now. If the bleeding does not slow after 10 minutes of firm pressure, it is an emergency.
chunks.source: WHO / International Federation of Red Cross basic first aid guidance

chunks.title: Burns
steps: Stop the burning. If the person is on fire, cover them with a blanket or heavy cloth to smother the flames.
Cool the burn under cool running water for at least 20 minutes. Do not use ice.
Remove rings, watches and tight clothing before swelling starts, unless stuck to the skin.
Cover loosely with cling film or a clean, non-fluffy cloth.
Do not burst blisters, do not apply toothpaste, oil, butter or ice, and do not pull off fabric stuck to the burn.
chunks.source: WHO burn care guidance / Red Cross first aid

chunks.title: Fractures and suspected breaks
steps: Do not try to straighten the limb.
Support the injured part in the position found. Pad around it with soft material.
If it helps, secure the limb to the uninjured part of the body with broad cloth.
Apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth for up to 20 minutes to reduce swelling.
Get medical help. Do not let the person eat or drink, in case they need an operation.

chunks.title: CPR — adult (basic)
steps: Check the person responds. Tap their shoulders and shout.
Check breathing normally. Look, listen and feel for up to 10 seconds.
If they are not breathing normally, send someone for help and get an AED if one is nearby.
Place both hands in the centre of the chest, between the nipples. Press down about 5 cm, fast and hard, about twice a second.
Keep going until the person breathes normally, help arrives, or you are too exhausted to continue.
chunks.source: WHO basic life support principles / Resuscitation Council UK lay guidance. NOTE: exact compression depth and rate vary by national body — confirm before publishing.

chunks.title: Drowning and floodwater rescue
steps: Do not enter moving or unknown-depth water to attempt a rescue. Reach or throw, never go.
Call for help immediately and get a life ring, long pole or rope if available.
Once out of the water, check breathing and start CPR if they are not breathing normally.
Keep the person warm and on their side if breathing, in case they vomit.
Every submersion needs medical assessment, even if the person seems fine afterwards.
chunks.source: WHO drowning prevention / Red Cross water rescue guidance

chunks.title: Heat exhaustion
steps: Move the person to a cool, shaded place.
Loosen heavy clothing.
Give cool water to sip if they are fully awake and not vomiting.
Cool the skin with damp cloth or fan them.
If they do not improve within 30 minutes, treat it as heatstroke.
chunks.source: WHO heat–health guidance / Indian Council of Medical Research heatwave advice

chunks.title: Heatstroke
steps: This is a life-threatening emergency. Move the person to shade and cool them immediately.
Remove excess clothing and wet the skin with cool water, then fan them hard.
Apply cold packs to the neck, armpits and groin.
Give cool water only if they are fully awake and swallowing normally.
Call for emergency help now. Confusion, collapse or very hot skin means heatstroke, not heat exhaustion.
chunks.source: WHO heat–health guidance / Indian Council of Medical Research heatwave advice

chunks.title: Hypothermia (too cold)
steps: Move the person somewhere warm, out of the wind and rain.
Remove wet clothing and replace with dry clothes, blankets or coats.
Warm gradually. Do not rub the limbs and do not use direct heat or very hot water.
Give a warm sweet drink if they are awake and able to swallow.
Handle gently and keep them lying still. Hypothermia can follow a flood rescue when the person is wet and wind-exposed.
chunks.source: Red Cross / NHS cold-weather first aid guidance

chunks.title: Snake bite
steps: Move away from the snake. Do not try to catch or kill it.
Keep the person still and calm. Movement spreads venom faster.
Rest the bitten limb, keeping it below heart level.
Remove rings, watches and tight clothing from the limb before swelling starts.
Do not cut the wound, do not suck out venom, and do not apply a tight tourniquet or ice. Call emergency services and get to hospital immediately.
chunks.source: WHO snakebite management guidance / Indian Council of Medical Research

chunks.title: Electric shock
steps: Do not touch the person while they are in contact with electricity or standing water.
Switch off the power at the mains first. Only if you cannot, push them clear with dry, non-conductive material such as wood or plastic.
Once free of the current, check breathing and start CPR if they are not breathing normally.
Any electric shock, even one that feels minor, needs medical assessment — the heart rhythm can be affected later.
Assume all nearby wiring is live until it is officially confirmed safe.
chunks.source: Red Cross first aid guidance / electrical safety first aid

chunks.title: Severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis)
steps: Call emergency help immediately. This can kill within minutes.
Use the person's own adrenaline auto-injector if they have one, into the outer mid-thigh.
Lie them flat with legs raised, unless they are having trouble breathing, in which case let them sit up.
If there is no breathing or pulse, start CPR.
Stay with them. Symptoms can return within 10–15 minutes, so a second dose may be needed if they carry one.
chunks.source: World Allergy Organization / Resuscitation Council UK anaphylaxis guidance

chunks.title: Fainting
steps: Lay the person flat on their back.
Raise their legs about 30 cm above the body.
Loosen tight clothing and make sure the area is ventilated.
They should recover within a minute or two. Give water once fully awake.
If they do not recover within a minute, are injured by the fall, or it happens again, call for medical help.

chunks.title: Choking
steps: Ask if they can cough. If they can cough forcefully, encourage them to keep coughing.
If they cannot speak, breathe or cough, give 5 firm blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
Then give 5 abdominal thrusts: fist above the navel, grasp with the other hand, pull sharply inwards and upwards.
Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object comes out or they become unresponsive.
If they become unresponsive, call emergency help and start CPR. Do not sweep the mouth blindly with a finger.
chunks.source: Red Cross choking guidance / Resuscitation Council UK

chunks.title: Flood safety — do not walk or drive through floodwater
steps: Never walk or drive through floodwater, even if it looks shallow. Moving water that is knee deep can knock a person over; 30 cm of fast water can carry away a car.
Do not drive through water of unknown depth. Turn around and find another route.
Stay away from fast-moving water, culverts, bridges, storm drains and underpasses.
If you are caught in a vehicle in moving water, stay inside. Get out and move to higher ground only if the water is not rising.
Watch for electrical cables and treat any water you cannot see the bottom of as live.
chunks.source: FEMA / Indian National Disaster Management Authority public flood safety guidance

chunks.title: Cyclone and severe storm safety
steps: Move indoors and stay away from windows and glass doors.
Stay on the ground floor or in an inner room, not on a roof or balcony.
Keep away from the coast, the beach and any area with trees or loose structures.
Charge your phone, keep a torch and power bank ready, and note your shelter location now — not during the event.
Do not attempt to travel during the storm. Wait for the official all-clear.
chunks.source: IMD cyclone safety guidance / NDMA public preparedness guidance

chunks.title: What to pack for a storm or evacuation
steps: Water: at least 1 litre per person per day, plus a small extra supply.
Power: a charged power bank, a torch and spare batteries.
Documents: passport, insurance and any medication details, kept in a waterproof bag.
Health: a few days of any regular prescription medication, plus basic first aid items.
Clothing and food: one change of clothes, high-visibility clothing if you have it, dry food that needs no cooking, and a small cash note.

chunks.title: Finding a safe shelter
steps: Move to higher ground. Avoid low-lying land, riverbanks, canals, underpasses and basements.
Stay clear of the coast, the beach and any flood-prone zone named in an alert.
Choose a sturdy building on high ground, or a designated shelter if you know one.
Take your phone, water, medication and documents with you.
Tell someone where you are going and register as safe with your accommodation or family.
chunks.source: NDMA public flood preparedness guidance / Kavach pilot content

trees.question: Is the person bleeding heavily and continuously?

options.label: Yes, blood is flowing or soaking the cloth
No, it is only a graze or minor cut

trees.question: You have pressed firmly for 10 minutes. Has the bleeding slowed?

options.label: Yes, it has slowed or stopped

terminalSteps: This is an emergency. Keep pressing hard and do not lift the cloth to check.
Call for emergency help now and stay with the person until help arrives.
Keep them warm and lying still. Do not give food or drink.

trees.question: You have stopped the bleeding. What is the next step?

options.label: The wound is small and clean
The wound is deep, gaping, or dirt is embedded

terminalSteps: Rinse the wound with clean water and cover it with a clean dressing.
Get medical help today if the wound is deep, gaping, dirty, or if the cut was caused by a rusty or dirty object.

trees.question: Does the person respond when you tap their shoulders and shout?
Are they breathing normally (look, listen and feel for up to 10 seconds)?

options.label: No, not breathing or only gasping

terminalSteps: Call for emergency help now and send someone for an AED.
Start chest compressions: hands in the centre of the chest, press hard and fast about twice a second.
Keep going until they breathe normally, help arrives, or you are too exhausted to continue.

trees.question: They are breathing. What next?
terminalSteps: Roll them onto their side into the recovery position.
Keep watching their breathing until help arrives.
If they stop breathing normally, start chest compressions again.

trees.question: They are awake. What should you focus on?
terminalSteps: Leave them sitting or lying where they are, and do not give them anything to eat or drink.
Watch them closely. If they become unresponsive, check breathing and start CPR.
Get medical help as soon as possible.

trees.question: Have you pulled the person out of the water safely?

options.label: Yes, they are out of the water
No, they are still in the water

terminalSteps: Do not enter moving or unknown-depth water to attempt a rescue.
Reach or throw, never go. Call for help and bring a life ring, long pole or rope.
Wait for trained rescuers. Your own safety comes first.

trees.question: Are they breathing normally?

options.label: No, not breathing or only gasping

terminalSteps: Start chest compressions immediately, the same as for CPR.
Send someone to call emergency help and get an AED.
Keep going until they breathe normally or help arrives.

trees.question: They are breathing after submersion. What next?
terminalSteps: Keep them warm, lying on their side, and watch their breathing.
Every submersion needs a medical assessment, even if they now seem fine. Get to hospital.
Watch for breathing problems for the rest of the day.

trees.question: Is the person confused, collapsed, or is their skin very hot to the touch?

options.label: No, they are alert and sweating

terminalSteps: This is heatstroke and it is life-threatening. Move them into shade and cool them immediately.
Remove excess clothing, wet the skin with cool water, and fan hard. Use cold packs on neck, armpits and groin.
Call for emergency help now.

trees.question: They are alert and sweating. What do you do?
terminalSteps: Move them to a cool, shaded place and loosen heavy clothing.
Give cool water to sip if they are fully awake and not vomiting.
If they do not improve within 30 minutes, or become confused, treat it as heatstroke and call for help.

trees.question: Do they have swelling of the face or throat, difficulty breathing, or a widespread rash with vomiting?

options.label: No, it is a mild local reaction

terminalSteps: This is anaphylaxis. Call emergency help immediately — it can be fatal within minutes.
Use their own adrenaline auto-injector into the outer mid-thigh if they have one.
Lay them flat with legs raised, or let them sit up if breathing is difficult. Stay with them.

trees.question: It is a mild, local reaction. What next?
terminalSteps: Watch closely. Symptoms can worsen quickly.
If swelling, breathing difficulty, vomiting or a widespread rash develops, call emergency help and use their adrenaline auto-injector.
Stay with them for at least 15 minutes.
